Preserve Support, Not Correspondence: Dynamic Routing for Offline Reinforcement Learning

Zhancun Mu Affiliation: School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University    Guangyu Zhao Affiliation: School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University    Yiwu Zhong Affiliation: School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University    Chi Zhang Email: {muzhancun,zhaogy24}@stu.pku.edu.cnyiwu-zhong@outlook.com  chizhang.cz@pku.edu.cn† Correspondence to: chizhang.cz@pku.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University
Abstract

One-step offline RL actors are attractive because they avoid backpropagating through long iterative samplers and keep inference cheap, but they still have to improve under a critic without drifting away from actions that the dataset can support. In recent one-step extraction pipelines, a strong iterative teacher provides one target action for each latent draw, and the same student output is asked to do both jobs: move toward higher Q and stay near that paired endpoint. If those two directions disagree, the loss resolves them as a compromise on that same sample, even when a nearby better action remains locally supported by the data. We propose DROL, a latent-conditioned one-step actor trained with top-1 dynamic routing. For each state, the actor samples KK candidate actions from a bounded latent prior, assigns each dataset action to its nearest candidate, and updates only that winner with bc (bc) and critic guidance. Because the routing is recomputed from the current candidate geometry, ownership of a supported region can shift across candidates over the course of learning. This gives a one-step actor room to make local improvements that pointwise extraction struggles to capture, while retaining single-pass inference at test time. On OGBench and D4RL, DROL is competitive with the one-step FQL baseline, improving many OGBench task groups while remaining strong on both AntMaze and Adroit. Project page: https://muzhancun.github.io/preprints/DROL.

1 Introduction

Offline rl (rl) requires improving a policy while staying within the action regions supported by a fixed dataset (Levine et al., 2020). This requirement becomes harder to satisfy on multimodal benchmarks such as OGBench (Park et al., 2025a), where nearby states can admit several distinct yet reasonable actions. Generative actors are attractive in this regime because they represent such multimodal behavior better than standard unimodal policies (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Lipman et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023; Park et al., 2025b).

Many strong generative offline rl methods rely on iterative sampling during training, inference, or both (Wang et al., 2023; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023; Espinosa-Dice et al., 2025; Mu et al., 2026). A one-step actor is attractive because it avoids backpropagating through a long iterative sampler and keeps execution cheap. One common way to obtain such an actor, exemplified by FQL (Park et al., 2025b), is to distill a stronger iterative teacher: for a latent draw zz, the teacher produces a~=μψ​(s,z)\tilde{a}=\mu_{\psi}(s,z), and the student output fθ​(s,z)f_{\theta}(s,z) is trained to improve Q while staying close to a~\tilde{a}. The difficulty is structural: within each update, the same sampled output must serve both roles. It is pushed toward higher Q while simultaneously being pulled back toward its paired teacher endpoint a~\tilde{a}. When these two directions disagree, the loss resolves the conflict by compromising on that same sample.

For a multimodal actor, different samples can naturally cover different supported modes. The key question is whether that ownership can shift during training. If it cannot, a sampled output remains responsible for its original endpoint even when a nearby supported improvement is available. If it can, that sample may move toward the better action while another takes over the old region. In FQL-style extraction, ownership stays attached to the same sampled output. In DROL, it can transfer across candidates. This tension is illustrated in Figure 1.

DROL retains the cheap one-step actor but changes the regularizer. For each state, it samples KK candidate actions, routes each dataset action to its nearest candidate,

k∗​(s,a)=arg⁡mink∈[K]⁡‖a^k−a‖22,k^{*}(s,a)=\arg\min_{k\in[K]}\|\hat{a}^{k}-a\|_{2}^{2},

and updates only that winner with behavior cloning and Q-improvement. As shown in Figure 1, one candidate can move toward a better local action while another retains ownership of the old supported region. The key difference from FQL-style extraction is that the behavior-cloning pull can change owners across candidates rather than remaining attached to a single sampled output. This design allows different latent regions to specialize to different parts of local support while preserving one-step inference at test time.

Our main contributions are:

  1. •

    We identify pointwise latent-to-teacher correspondence as an unnecessary constraint in one-step extraction for multimodal offline rl, and argue that local action support is the object worth preserving.

  2. •

    We propose DROL, a routed candidate-set actor that samples multiple actions during training, assigns each data action to its nearest candidate, and updates only the routed winner.

  3. •

    We analyze the mechanism of routing, including non-collapse, responsibility transfer, and the role of the routing budget KK, and evaluate the resulting one-step actor on OGBench and D4RL (Fu et al., 2020) with routing visualizations and KK ablations.

2 Preliminaries and Problem Setup

We consider an mdp (mdp) (𝒮,𝒜,r,p,γ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},r,p,\gamma) together with a fixed offline dataset 𝒟={(s,a,r,s′)}\mathcal{D}=\{(s,a,r,s^{\prime})\}. Given a critic QϕQ_{\phi}, the actor should seek high-value actions while staying close to the state-conditional action regions supported by the data. At an abstract level, offline rl can be written as

maxπθ\displaystyle\max_{\pi_{\theta}} 𝔼s∼𝒟,a∼πθ(⋅|s)[Qϕ(s,a)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D},\,a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|s)}[Q_{\phi}(s,a)] (1)
s.t.\displaystyle\textrm{s.t.} 𝔻(πθ(⋅|s),πβ(⋅|s))≤ϵ,\displaystyle\mathbb{D}\bigl(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|s),\pi_{\beta}(\cdot|s)\bigr)\leq\epsilon,

where πβ\pi_{\beta} denotes the implicit behavior distribution and 𝔻\mathbb{D} is a discrepancy that keeps policy improvement within trustworthy regions. In the multimodal setting studied here, exact duplicates at a single observation are rare, so we instead search within a small neighborhood of states around ss rather than relying on literal repeated supervision at the exact same state. For this paper, the central question is which object the regularizer is actually trying to preserve.

We train the critic with the usual Bellman regression objective

ℒQ​(ϕ)=𝔼(s,a,r,s′)∼𝒟​[(Qϕ​(s,a)−(r+γ​Qϕ¯​(s′,πθ​(s′))))2],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{Q}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,r,s^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D}}\Bigl[\bigl(Q_{\phi}(s,a)-(r+\gamma Q_{\bar{\phi}}(s^{\prime},\pi_{\theta}(s^{\prime})))\bigr)^{2}\Bigr], (2)

so the main design question is concentrated in the actor update.

Positioning relative to prior work.

Among generative offline rl methods, FQL (Park et al., 2025b) is the clearest reference point, since it also trains a one-step actor from a stronger iterative teacher. DROL departs from that line at the level of the regularizer: the key issue for us is the pointwise latent-conditioned tether used during extraction. ReFORM (Zhang et al., 2026) is related in a different way. It also argues that support should be preserved in offline rl, but does so through reflected flow constructions rather than routed candidate sets. Finally, the routed behavior-cloning update is closest to imle (imle) (Li and Malik, 2019) and imle Policy (Rana et al., 2025), which also rely on nearest-sample or set-level matching. What is new here is using that matching primitive as the actor-side support regularizer, coupled directly to local Q-improvement. See Appendix B for a broader discussion of adjacent generative offline rl and policy-learning methods.

2.1 Pointwise-Correspondence One-Step Extraction

Many recent generative offline rl methods, most notably FQL (Park et al., 2025b), use a strong iterative model μψ\mu_{\psi} as a behavior policy and then train a cheaper one-step actor fθf_{\theta} for critic-guided optimization. The teacher can be instantiated as a flow, diffusion, or other latent-conditioned generator; the precise architecture matters less here than the structure of the extracted actor loss.

Let z∼p0z\sim p_{0} be a latent variable shared by the teacher and student, and let a~=μψ​(s,z)\tilde{a}=\mu_{\psi}(s,z) be the teacher action associated with (s,z)(s,z). A common extraction template is

ℒπ​(θ)=𝔼s,z​[−Qϕ​(s,fθ​(s,z))+α​ℓ​(fθ​(s,z),a~)],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\pi}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{s,z}\Bigl[-Q_{\phi}(s,f_{\theta}(s,z))+\alpha\,\ell\bigl(f_{\theta}(s,z),\tilde{a}\bigr)\Bigr], (3)

where ℓ\ell is a distillation loss such as squared error. This objective is practical because it avoids differentiating through the teacher’s full sampling process. It also imposes a pointwise correspondence: for each sampled pair (s,z)(s,z), the same student output fθ​(s,z)f_{\theta}(s,z) is trained toward the teacher endpoint a~=μψ​(s,z)\tilde{a}=\mu_{\psi}(s,z) associated with that latent. The endpoint may shift with ss and with the teacher parameters over training, but within the current gradient the Q term and the distillation term remain attached to that same sampled output. That output therefore has to absorb the tradeoff on its own: if moving toward a higher-Q action pushes it away from a~\tilde{a}, the same update pulls it back.

This is the structural foil for DROL. If the critic prefers a nearby action that remains well supported by the dataset, Equation 3 provides no second sampled output that can take over the old teacher-linked region. DROL retains the tractable one-step actor setup but replaces samplewise teacher-student alignment with set-level routing over the actor’s current candidate actions.

3 Dynamic Routing for Offline RL

3.1 Actor as a Candidate Set

We start from a latent-conditioned actor fθ​(s,z)f_{\theta}(s,z). The local support around ss is not observed directly, and exact support inclusion is intractable for a continuous generative actor. DROL therefore routes over a sampled candidate set drawn from the actor itself; the separate local-support object is used only in the conceptual discussion and visualization.

For each state ss, we sample KK latent codes and generate

a^k=fθ(s,zk),zk∼Unif(BRdz),k=1,…,K,\hat{a}^{k}=f_{\theta}(s,z_{k}),\qquad z_{k}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(B_{R}^{d_{z}}),\qquad k=1,\dots,K, (4)

where dzd_{z} is the latent dimension and BRdzB_{R}^{d_{z}} is the dzd_{z}-dimensional Euclidean ball of radius RR. Following ReFORM (Zhang et al., 2026), we adopt the dimension-aware choice R=daR=\sqrt{d_{a}} in our experiments, where dad_{a} is the action dimension. With this choice, the overall latent scale stays on the same order as the action dimension (see Section C.5). These samples form the candidate set

Aθ​(s)={a^1,…,a^K}.A_{\theta}(s)=\{\hat{a}^{1},\dots,\hat{a}^{K}\}. (5)

A larger candidate set exposes more local directions to the routing rule simultaneously, enabling specialization and subsequent handoff during training.

The choice R=daR=\sqrt{d_{a}} ties the latent scale to the action geometry rather than fixing a single radius across tasks, while keeping the prior isotropic. Compared with an unbounded Gaussian prior, Unif⁡(BRdz)\mathrm{Unif}(B_{R}^{d_{z}}) removes heavy-tail latent excursions and keeps the sampled candidate set compact, which is better aligned with a routing-based local support surrogate. At test time, the policy uses only a single latent sample,

πθ​(s)=fθ​(s,z),z∼Unif⁡(BRdz),\pi_{\theta}(s)=f_{\theta}(s,z),\qquad z\sim\mathrm{Unif}(B_{R}^{d_{z}}), (6)

so the multiplicity KK is purely a training-time device. After training, a single latent draw already samples from the reorganized actor, so execution stays within the plain one-step setting.

3.2 Top-1 Dynamic Routing

For each offline pair (s,a)(s,a), DROL routes the dataset action to its current nearest candidate,

k∗​(s,a)=arg⁡mink∈[K]⁡‖a^k−a‖22.k^{*}(s,a)=\arg\min_{k\in[K]}\|\hat{a}^{k}-a\|_{2}^{2}. (7)

Only the routed winner a^k∗​(s,a)\hat{a}^{k^{*}(s,a)} receives the actor update for that data point. Routing is recomputed from the current candidate geometry at every gradient step, and gradients are not propagated through the discrete arg⁡min\arg\min itself.

The actor objective is

ℒactor(θ)=𝔼(s,a)∼𝒟,z1:K[∥a^k∗​(s,a)−a∥22−αQϕ(s,a^k∗​(s,a))].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{actor}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim\mathcal{D},\,z_{1:K}}\Bigl[\|\hat{a}^{k^{*}(s,a)}-a\|_{2}^{2}-\alpha Q_{\phi}\bigl(s,\hat{a}^{k^{*}(s,a)}\bigr)\Bigr]. (8)

The first term is winner-only bc. It anchors the currently responsible candidate to the local data neighborhood that routing assigns to it. The second term performs critic-guided improvement on that same candidate. Because both terms act on the same routed prototype, bc becomes a local support surrogate rather than a global penalty on the full actor.

The critic is trained with the standard Bellman loss

ℒQ​(ϕ)=𝔼(s,a,r,s′)∼𝒟​[(Qϕ​(s,a)−(r+γ​Qϕ¯​(s′,πθ​(s′))))2].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{Q}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,r,s^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D}}\Bigl[\bigl(Q_{\phi}(s,a)-(r+\gamma Q_{\bar{\phi}}(s^{\prime},\pi_{\theta}(s^{\prime})))\bigr)^{2}\Bigr]. (9)

Routing determines how support is regularized during actor learning, while execution and critic targets remain those of an ordinary one-sample policy.

3.3 Interpretation

Top-1 routing induces a state-conditional Euclidean Voronoi partition over the candidate set (Aurenhammer, 1991; Okabe et al., 2000). Given Aθ​(s)={a^1,…,a^K}A_{\theta}(s)=\{\hat{a}^{1},\dots,\hat{a}^{K}\}, the cell of candidate kk is

Vk(s):={a∈ℝda:∥a^k−a∥22≤∥a^j−a∥22,∀j∈[K]}.V_{k}(s):=\left\{a\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}:\|\hat{a}^{k}-a\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|\hat{a}^{j}-a\|_{2}^{2},\ \forall j\in[K]\right\}. (10)

The cells {Vk​(s)}k=1K\{V_{k}(s)\}_{k=1}^{K} partition the action space up to measure-zero tie boundaries, and the routing rule returns the index of the cell containing the dataset action. Each dataset action therefore supervises only the candidate whose current cell contains it, and each candidate is responsible only for the portion of the local support that currently falls within its cell, namely Vk​(s)∩supplocal​(s)V_{k}(s)\cap\mathrm{supp}_{\mathrm{local}}(s) in the idealized local-support picture. If one candidate moves toward a better local action, another can inherit responsibility for the old neighborhood as soon as the nearest-neighbor partition changes. Iterative policies revisit several actions at inference time; DROL revisits several actions only during actor training. Once latent regions have specialized, execution returns to ordinary one-sample generation.

4 Three Insights Behind DROL

This section is organized around the three questions that tend to come up first. Will winner-only routing collapse the candidates? Why can one candidate move without immediately destroying support elsewhere? Why does a larger routing budget KK help on some task families? The statements below are intentionally local: they are meant to explain the actor update rather than prove global rl convergence. Proofs are deferred to Appendix C.

4.1 A Separated-Demand Toy Model Does Not Collapse

It is helpful to begin with a small dispatch model. Imagine a fixed local state neighborhood in which action demand concentrates around several separated regions. Each candidate acts like a rider serving the orders closest to it. If two riders wait in the same neighborhood while another neighborhood has none, the average service distance increases. Winner-only routing therefore behaves like local specialization rather than global averaging.

Proposition 4.1 (Separated Neighborhoods Avoid Collapse).

Let

ρ=1M​∑m=1MUnif⁡(Im)\rho=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathrm{Unif}(I_{m})

be a one-dimensional action distribution supported on disjoint intervals

Im=[cm−r,cm+r],m=1,…,M,I_{m}=[c_{m}-r,c_{m}+r],\qquad m=1,\dots,M,

with gaps cm+1−cm>4​rc_{m+1}-c_{m}>4r. For K=MK=M, consider the routed behavior-cloning objective

𝒥(a^1:K):=∫mink∈[K]|a^k−a|2ρ(da).\mathcal{J}(\hat{a}_{1:K}):=\int\min_{k\in[K]}|\hat{a}_{k}-a|^{2}\,\rho(\mathrm{d}a).

Then every global minimizer of 𝒥\mathcal{J} places exactly one prototype in each interval ImI_{m}. In particular, a collapsed configuration with two prototypes in one interval and none in another cannot be optimal.

This toy model addresses the main collapse objection. Winner-only bc does not pull all candidates toward the same point. When the local support contains separated neighborhoods, the routed reconstruction loss prefers one candidate per neighborhood. That is precisely the mechanism we want from DROL. The visualization in Figure 2 should be read in this spirit: the candidate set spreads to cover a local support cloud before subsequent updates refine it.

4.2 Routing Replaces a Persistent Tether with a Transferable Anchor

Consider the gap between a pointwise-correspondence loss and a routed loss for a single supported target aa at state ss. Under pointwise distillation, aa can be read as the designated teacher endpoint for a sampled latent-state pair. Under routing, it is the local target currently assigned to the winning candidate. For a single candidate xx, the pointwise-correspondence objective is

ℓfix​(x,a)=‖x−a‖22−α​Qϕ​(s,x).\ell_{\mathrm{fix}}(x;a)=\|x-a\|_{2}^{2}-\alpha Q_{\phi}(s,x).

For a routed candidate set A=(x1,…,xK)A=(x_{1},\dots,x_{K}), define

ℓroute​(A,a)=mink∈[K]⁡‖xk−a‖22−α​Qϕ​(s,xk∗​(a)),k∗​(a)=arg⁡mink⁡‖xk−a‖22.\ell_{\mathrm{route}}(A;a)=\min_{k\in[K]}\|x_{k}-a\|_{2}^{2}\;-\;\alpha Q_{\phi}\bigl(s,x_{k^{*}(a)}\bigr),\qquad k^{*}(a)=\arg\min_{k}\|x_{k}-a\|_{2}^{2}.
Proposition 4.2 (Persistent Tether versus Routed Anchor).

For the pointwise-correspondence objective,

∇xℓfix​(x,a)=2​(x−a)−α​∇xQϕ​(s,x),\nabla_{x}\ell_{\mathrm{fix}}(x;a)=2(x-a)-\alpha\nabla_{x}Q_{\phi}(s,x),

so the sample aa continues to exert the same pullback term 2​(x−a)2(x-a) regardless of what other candidates may exist. For the routed objective, if the winner k∗​(a)k^{*}(a) is unique, then

∇xiℓroute​(A,a)=0for all ​i≠k∗​(a),\nabla_{x_{i}}\ell_{\mathrm{route}}(A;a)=0\qquad\text{for all }i\neq k^{*}(a),

and

∇xk∗​(a)ℓroute​(A,a)=2​(xk∗​(a)−a)−α​∇xQϕ​(s,xk∗​(a)).\nabla_{x_{k^{*}(a)}}\ell_{\mathrm{route}}(A;a)=2(x_{k^{*}(a)}-a)-\alpha\nabla_{x}Q_{\phi}(s,x_{k^{*}(a)}).

Once another candidate becomes the nearest one to aa, this behavior-cloning contribution transfers to the new winner.

Proposition 4.3 (Pointwise Correspondence Biases a Local Improvement).

Let U⊂ℝdaU\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} be convex, let Qϕ​(s,⋅)Q_{\phi}(s,\cdot) be differentiable and mm-strongly concave on UU, and let xQ∈Ux_{Q}\in U be an interior maximizer of Qϕ​(s,⋅)Q_{\phi}(s,\cdot) over UU. For a target a∈Ua\in U, define

g⁡(x)=‖x−a‖22−α​Qϕ​(s,x),x∈U.g(x)=\|x-a\|_{2}^{2}-\alpha Q_{\phi}(s,x),\qquad x\in U.

Then gg has a unique minimizer xfixx_{\mathrm{fix}}. Moreover:

  1. •

    xQx_{Q} is stationary for gg if and only if a=xQa=x_{Q}.

  2. •

    The minimizer satisfies

    ‖xfix−xQ‖2≤22+α​m​‖a−xQ‖2.\|x_{\mathrm{fix}}-x_{Q}\|_{2}\leq\frac{2}{2+\alpha m}\|a-x_{Q}\|_{2}.

The partition matters because it determines which candidate receives the pullback from a supported target. Under pointwise teacher distillation, the same sampled latent-state pair keeps paying to stay near its designated teacher endpoint. Under routing, that pullback is attached to the current winner of the nearest-neighbor partition, and when the partition changes, the pullback changes owner with it.

The second proposition makes the local consequence explicit. Even when the inherited target aa and the local Q-favored action xQx_{Q} lie in the same supported neighborhood, xQx_{Q} is not stationary under a pointwise-correspondence loss unless a=xQa=x_{Q}. The optimizer therefore settles at a compromise between the old target and the critic-preferred action. Routed training does not eliminate the behavior-cloning term, but it allows another candidate to take over the old neighborhood once the partition changes. This is the local mechanism that enables a one-step actor to follow the critic more freely without dropping support.

4.3 Larger KK Improves Handoff Availability

The final question is why a larger routing budget helps on some task families. For a fixed state ss, suppose the local support is covered by modal neighborhoods U1​(s),…,UMs​(s)U_{1}(s),\dots,U_{M_{s}}(s). Let

pm​(s):=ℙz∼Unif⁡(BRdz)​(fθ​(s,z)∈Um​(s)),p_{m}(s):=\mathbb{P}_{z\sim\mathrm{Unif}(B_{R}^{d_{z}})}\bigl(f_{\theta}(s,z)\in U_{m}(s)\bigr),

so that pm​(s)p_{m}(s) is the probability that one sampled candidate lands in neighborhood mm.

Proposition 4.4 (Coverage from Larger Candidate Sets).

If pm​(s)>0p_{m}(s)>0 for all m=1,…,Msm=1,\dots,M_{s}, then

ℙ(∀m,∃k∈[K],a^k∈Um(s))≥1−∑m=1Ms(1−pm(s))K.\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\forall m,\exists k\in[K],\hat{a}_{k}\in U_{m}(s)\Bigr)\geq 1-\sum_{m=1}^{M_{s}}(1-p_{m}(s))^{K}.

In particular, letting pmin​(s):=minm⁡pm​(s)p_{\min}(s):=\min_{m}p_{m}(s),

ℙ⁡(∀m,∃k,a^k∈Um​(s))≥1−Ms​e−K​pmin​(s).\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\forall m,\exists k,\hat{a}_{k}\in U_{m}(s)\Bigr)\geq 1-M_{s}e^{-Kp_{\min}(s)}.

This is not a coverage-creation statement. Increasing KK does not invent new supported actions; it only makes it less likely that the current candidate set misses neighborhoods that are already reachable. That matters because responsibility transfer only works if another candidate is available nearby to take over. This is the geometric role of KK in DROL.

5 Experiments

We use experiments to answer three practical questions on OGBench (Park et al., 2025a), supported by additional results on D4RL (Fu et al., 2020). First, can routing make a plain one-step actor competitive with heavier iterative policies on multimodal offline RL tasks? Second, do the candidate sets exhibit the non-collapse, specialization, handoff, and locally stable regimes suggested by Section 4? Third, how does the routing budget KK affect this behavior?

5.1 Main Results on OGBench and D4RL

Table 1 summarizes the main benchmark results. DROL executes with a single latent draw and no multi-step refinement at test time. Even under this restriction, the fixed default configuration DROL(16) matches or improves over the one-step FQL baseline on 6 of the 10 OGBench task groups, with especially clear gains on antmaze-large, humanoidmaze-medium, antsoccer, and cube-single. Selecting KK once on a representative default task within each OGBench task family and reusing it across the remaining tasks yields DROL∗, which matches or improves over FQL on 9 of the 10 OGBench groups. The largest gain appears on antmaze-giant, where the family average rises from 99 for FQL and 33 for the default configuration to 4545 after tuning only KK. The D4RL rows tell a complementary story on a more established benchmark suite: DROL matches FQL on Adroit and remains close on AntMaze, suggesting that the routed one-step actor transfers beyond OGBench rather than fitting a single benchmark family.

Taken together, the table supports a narrow claim: once the actor is no longer forced to preserve pointwise teacher correspondence during extraction, a simple one-step policy can already recover a large fraction of the performance that otherwise appears to require heavier inference. The runtime comparison in Figure 3 tells the same story from the systems side: DROL keeps one-step inference cost essentially at the FQL level while iterative baselines remain substantially slower, and its candidate evaluations are easy to batch across KK during training.

5.2 Mechanism Study: Voronoi Evolution During Training

Figure 2 visualizes the mechanism on a fixed representative state. Because exact repeated actions at a single observation are rare, the local support object in the discussion is approximated by a dense surrogate at that state, while the figure itself overlays only the current candidate set and its induced Voronoi cells {Vk​(s)}k=1K\{V_{k}(s)\}_{k=1}^{K} from Section 3. The figure checks three concrete predictions from Section 4: the candidate set should spread rather than collapse, one common regime is responsibility reassignment, and another is stable optimization with an unchanged winner. The second and third panels should therefore be read as two representative phases of routed training rather than a strict chronology.

5.3 No Collapse and Capacity Scaling with KK

Figure 3 complements the geometric picture with three training metrics on representative environments. Cand. Pairwise Dist. averages ‖a^i−a^j‖22/da\|\hat{a}_{i}-\hat{a}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}/d_{a} over off-diagonal pairs, the inset log10⁡(Cand. Div.)\log_{10}(\text{Cand.\ Div.}) shows mean centroid divergence ‖a^k−a¯‖22/da\|\hat{a}_{k}-\bar{a}\|_{2}^{2}/d_{a}, and the red curve is the routed bc loss.

Two trends are consistent across all three environments. First, the candidate set does not collapse as KK grows. Both the pairwise spread and the centroid divergence increase with KK, indicating that the additional candidates organize into distinct local actions rather than redundant copies. Second, the routed bc loss decreases with KK. This is the scaling one would expect if a larger candidate set provides a finer local quantization of the supported action neighborhood. Taken together with Figure 2, these curves support the picture in Section 4: routing uses larger candidate sets to build more local structure, not to replicate the same action multiple times.

5.4 Sensitivity to the Number of Candidates KK

Figure 4 shows that KK controls routing capacity rather than acting as a monotone scale parameter. Large or highly multimodal navigation families benefit most from larger candidate sets, while other families saturate earlier or prefer intermediate values of KK. In practice, fixing K=16K=16 already makes the workable range of α\alpha clear, so we tune α\alpha first and sweep KK only when additional budget is available.

6 Conclusion and Limitations

DROL studies one-step actor learning in multimodal offline rl from a geometric perspective. The actor produces a small candidate set, routing selects the candidate closest to the supported target, and responsibility can transfer as optimization progresses. This keeps local support neighborhoods intact while still allowing the actor to follow value improvements, and it is already sufficient for a plain one-sample policy to recover a substantial fraction of the performance typically associated with heavier iterative inference, while keeping deployment cost close to that of standard one-step baselines. In simple terms, routed training continually reconsiders which sampled action should represent the local data neighborhood, and that answer is allowed to change as better actions emerge.

Our theory is local and mechanism-oriented rather than a full convergence theory for offline rl, and the method still relies on a fixed routing budget KK, Euclidean matching, and additional training-time candidate evaluations whose cost grows with KK. These limitations point to several natural next steps: learned routing metrics, adaptive candidate budgets, softer responsibility sharing, and region-level regularization beyond pointwise targets. It is also worth investigating whether geometric constraints can better balance behavior cloning against Q-improvement, and whether best-of-NN sampling can further improve the resulting one-step policy.

Appendix A Implementation Details

We use the same offline training and evaluation pipeline as the one-step FQL baseline. For each state ss, DROL samples KK latent noises uniformly from the radius-da\sqrt{d_{a}} ball, maps them through a one-step vector field, and obtains KK candidate actions. The dataset action is routed to its nearest candidate under squared Euclidean distance, and both the bc term and the Q-improvement term are applied only to that winning candidate. All reported results use one-step inference. We do not use best-of-NN selection in training or evaluation.

For OGBench, DROL(16) keeps the default K=16K=16 in every family. For DROL∗, we choose one family-level routing budget K⋆K^{\star} on the representative task marked by (*) in Table 4 and reuse it for the other tasks in that family without changing any other hyperparameters. For D4RL, all runs use 500500K offline updates. The DROL∗ protocol is benchmark-specific. On D4RL Adroit, we sweep KK with the natural task families in mind (for example, pen-*, door-*, hammer-*, and relocate-*) and report the resulting choices in Table 3. On D4RL AntMaze, we select KK per task rather than once per family because the transfer between tasks is noticeably weaker. The table below summarizes the benchmark-level (α,K)(\alpha,K) settings. The right column is only used when DROL∗ differs from DROL(16).

Appendix B Related Work

Classical offline RL methods such as CQL [Kumar et al., 2020], TD3+BC [Fujimoto and Gu, 2021], and IQL [Kostrikov et al., 2022] control distribution shift mainly through critic-side pessimism or simple behavior regularization. As multimodal benchmarks such as OGBench have made actor expressiveness more important, recent work has increasingly turned to diffusion and flow policies, including Diffusion-QL [Wang et al., 2023], IDQL [Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023], and flow-matching-based generators built on Lipman et al. [2023].

DROL is most closely related to generative offline RL methods that focus on policy extraction once the critic is fixed or largely standard. FQL [Park et al., 2025b] is the clearest reference point: it learns an expressive flow teacher and distills it into a one-step actor for critic-guided optimization. MeanFlow-QL [Wang et al., 2025], SORL [Espinosa-Dice et al., 2025], FAC [Chae et al., 2026], and DeFlow [Mu et al., 2026] pursue adjacent efficiency or refinement strategies. Our departure from this family is not the specific teacher architecture, but the object being regularized during extraction: teacher-student objectives of this type typically preserve a pointwise latent-conditioned pairing between teacher endpoints and actor outputs, whereas DROL regularizes the actor’s current candidate set at the level of local supported neighborhoods.

Another closely related direction emphasizes support-aware flow design. ReFORM [Zhang et al., 2026] is especially relevant because it also argues that support, rather than generic distributional closeness, should be the operative constraint in offline RL, and it uses bounded and reflected flow constructions to preserve support by design. DROL is complementary in spirit but different in mechanism: rather than constraining policy improvement through a reflected flow transformation, it uses dynamic routing over a one-step candidate set and lets responsibility move between candidates as the local partition changes.

At the policy-learning level, the routed behavior-cloning term is most closely related to imle [Li and Malik, 2019] and to its policy instantiation in imle Policy [Rana et al., 2025]. These methods train a conditional generator through nearest-sample or set-level matching rather than pointwise sample-to-target correspondence, which is why they are the right comparison point for DROL’s winner-only bc objective. The novelty here is not the matching primitive itself, but its use as the support-aware regularizer coupled directly to local Q-improvement on the routed winner. DROL also differs from IBC [Florence et al., 2022], which models the policy implicitly with an energy-based objective rather than a direct latent-conditioned generator with hard routing during training.
